wrong: Taking advantage of superior strength to overpower the victim
That is abuse of superior strength, a separate qualifying circumstance. Treachery is about means that remove any risk from the victim's defense.
Deliberately choosing nighttime to commit the crime
That is nocturnity, a separate aggravating circumstance.
Planning the crime long before carrying it out
That is evident premeditation, not treachery.
Sudden attack giving the victim no chance to defend
That is treachery, not evident premeditation.
Killing committed in the heat of passion
That is passion or obfuscation, a mitigating circumstance and the opposite of cool reflection.
Committing the crime for a price or reward
That is the aggravating circumstance of price, reward or promise.
Commission of the crime at night in an uninhabited place
Nighttime and uninhabited place are separate aggravating circumstances, not treachery.
Use of superior strength out of proportion to the victim's
That is abuse of superior strength, a different circumstance that treachery absorbs when both are present.
Deliberate planning with sufficient time to reflect on the consequences
That is evident premeditation, not treachery.

keep: The correct answer is already the shortest option, and the other three are the real Miranda rights, so there is no length cue.

wrong: By Congress during invasion or rebellion
The power to suspend belongs to the President (Art. VII, Sec. 18). Congress may only revoke or extend the suspension.
By the President whenever public safety requires
Public safety alone is not enough; there must be actual invasion or rebellion AND public safety must require it.
By the Supreme Court upon petition of the President
The Supreme Court reviews the factual basis of a suspension; it does not suspend the writ.

keep: All four are real courts of similar length; the correct answer is not the longest.

wrong: Certified copies are always enough
Copies are allowed only in the exceptions under Rule 130, like loss or destruction of the original. The rule requires the original.
The most credible witness must testify
The rule is about documents, not the credibility of witnesses.
Physical evidence outweighs testimony
That is a general way of weighing evidence, not the best evidence rule.

keep: The options are all ages in the same form and the correct one is not noticeably longer; the wrong ages are real near-misses (18 is the age of majority, 9 was the old RPC limit).
flag: RA 9344, as amended, exempts a child FIFTEEN YEARS OF AGE OR UNDER at the time of the offense, so the answer Below 15 years old leaves out a child who is exactly 15. Consider changing it to 15 years old and below.

keep: The correct answer is in the middle by length, and the longest option (wrong because prohibited by law) is the real near-miss.

wrong: Acts wrong in themselves by nature
That is mala in se. Mala prohibita are wrong only because a law prohibits them.
Acts punished only when done with intent
Intent is generally immaterial in mala prohibita; doing the prohibited act is enough.
Acts punished under the Revised Penal Code
RPC felonies are generally mala in se; mala prohibita are mostly found in special penal laws.
Fault or negligence
That is culpa. Dolo means deliberate intent, or malice.
Lack of foresight
That is a form of imprudence, which belongs to culpa, not dolo.
Accident without fault
That is an exempting circumstance under Art. 12, not dolo.
Deceit or malice
That is dolo, the deliberate intent to do wrong.
Intent to commit a felony
Intent belongs to dolo. Culpa is wrongdoing through imprudence, negligence, lack of skill or foresight.
Accident without fault or intent
That is an exempting circumstance; culpa still involves fault.
Proposal by one person to another to commit a felony
That is proposal. Conspiracy needs both the agreement and the decision of two or more persons.
Cooperation in a felony by previous or simultaneous acts
That describes accomplices (Art. 18), who cooperate without being in conspiracy.
Concealing the effects of a felony after it was committed
That describes accessories (Art. 19).
Only the mastermind is liable
In conspiracy all conspirators are equally liable, whatever their part.
Each is liable for their own acts only
That is the rule without conspiracy. With conspiracy, the act of one is the act of all.
Penalty is lowered by one degree
Conspiracy does not lower the penalty. It is accomplices who get one degree lower.
Proposal to commit a crime
Proposal is made by one person; conspiracy needs the agreement of two or more.
Cooperation after the crime is committed
That describes accessories, not conspirators.
Mere presence at the scene of the crime
Mere presence, without agreement, does not make one a conspirator.
Agreeing with another to commit a crime
That is conspiracy. Proposal is when one who has decided to commit a felony proposes it to others.
Beginning the crime by overt acts
That is the attempted stage.
Planning a crime alone without telling anyone
Planning alone is not punishable; proposal needs another person.
May be justifying or exempting
Alternative circumstances affect the penalty only as mitigating or aggravating; they never justify or exempt.
Always aggravate the penalty
They aggravate only in some cases, depending on the nature and effects of the crime.
Always lower the penalty by one degree
That describes privileged mitigating circumstances. Alternative circumstances may mitigate or aggravate.
Mitigating circumstance only
Intoxication mitigates only when it is not habitual or intentional; when habitual or intentional it aggravates. That makes it alternative.
Aggravating circumstance only
Intoxication aggravates only when habitual or intentional; otherwise it mitigates.
Exempting circumstance
Intoxication never exempts; at most it mitigates.
Reclusion Temporal
That is the penalty for homicide (Art. 249).
Prision Mayor to Reclusion Temporal
That range is too low; murder is punished by reclusion perpetua to death under Art. 248.
Life Imprisonment to Death
Life imprisonment is the term used in special laws, not the RPC; the RPC penalty is reclusion perpetua.
flag: Art. 248 says reclusion perpetua to death, but RA 9346 (2006) prohibits imposing death, so courts now impose reclusion perpetua. Consider adding this to the explanation so students are not misled.

wrong: Presence of mitigating circumstances
Mitigating circumstances lower the penalty within a crime; qualifying circumstances change homicide into murder.
Relationship between offender and victim
Relationship makes the killing parricide, not murder.
Number of wounds inflicted
The number of wounds does not decide the crime; qualifying circumstances do.
When attended by generic aggravating circumstances
Generic aggravating circumstances raise the penalty within homicide but do not turn it into murder.
When the victim is the offender's spouse
That makes the killing parricide.
When multiple wounds are inflicted
The number of wounds alone does not make homicide murder.
Robbery and homicide charged as two separate crimes
Robbery with homicide is a single special complex crime, not two separate crimes.
Homicide committed first, with robbery as an afterthought
If the intent to take property came only after the killing, there are separate crimes, not robbery with homicide.
Killing of a person during a kidnapping
That is kidnapping with homicide, a different special complex crime.
Theft committed with violence against persons
Violence or intimidation makes it robbery, not theft.
Theft committed by a public officer of public funds
That is malversation (Art. 217).
Taking property through deceit that causes damage to the owner
That is estafa (Art. 315).
Crime against chastity requiring a private complaint
RA 8353 reclassified rape as a crime against persons, so it no longer needs a private complaint.
Carnal knowledge of a woman only, never of a man
RA 8353 added rape by sexual assault, which can be committed against any person, including men.
Unjust vexation of a sexual nature
Unjust vexation is a light felony; rape involves carnal knowledge or sexual assault through force, threat or intimidation.
Reclusion temporal
Art. 263 does not reach reclusion temporal; its highest penalty is prision mayor.
Arresto menor
Arresto menor is for slight physical injuries (Art. 266).
Destierro
Destierro is banishment, not a penalty for physical injuries under Art. 263.
flag: Art. 263 has four penalties depending on the injury: prision mayor only for insanity, imbecility, impotence or blindness; lower penalties (prision correccional, arresto mayor) for the other paragraphs. Consider rewording the question to name the first paragraph, e.g. serious physical injuries causing blindness.

wrong: Refusal to obey a lawful order of a person in authority
That is resistance and disobedience (Art. 151).
Rising publicly to prevent officials from performing duties
That is sedition (Art. 139).
Attack on a private person in a public place
The victim of direct assault must be a person in authority or an agent of one.
Attacking a person in authority on duty
That is direct assault, which involves force or serious intimidation.
Rising publicly to overthrow the government
That is rebellion.
Attacking someone who helps a person in authority
That is indirect assault (Art. 149).
Crime against property
Rape is not a property crime; RA 8353 classifies it as a crime against persons.
Crime against public order
Crimes against public order include rebellion and sedition, not rape.
Crime against chastity
Before RA 8353 rape was a crime against chastity; the law reclassified it as a crime against persons.
Reclusion perpetua to death
That range is for the gravest crimes, like murder or robbery with homicide.
Fine only, without imprisonment
Robbery always carries imprisonment; a fine alone is never its penalty.
Arresto menor or public censure
Those are light penalties for light felonies; robbery is a grave or less grave felony.
flag: The penalty depends on the article: Art. 299 (inhabited house) can reach reclusion temporal, while Art. 302 (uninhabited place) is prision correccional. Consider naming the article in the question.

wrong: Presence of generic aggravating circumstances
Generic aggravating circumstances raise the penalty but do not turn homicide into murder.
Intent to kill the victim
Intent to kill is present in both homicide and murder.
Kind of weapon that was used
The weapon does not decide the crime; qualifying circumstances do.
Killing of a child less than 7 days old
The law sets three days (72 hours); an older child's killing is parricide or murder, not infanticide.
Killing of a fetus inside the mother's womb
That is abortion (Arts. 256-259).
Killing of one's own legitimate child of any age
That is parricide (Art. 246).
After conviction by the RTC for any offense
After conviction by the RTC, bail becomes discretionary, not a matter of right.
Before conviction for offenses punished by reclusion perpetua
For these, bail is not a right when evidence of guilt is strong; it is decided after a hearing.
Only when the prosecutor agrees
Bail as a right does not depend on the prosecutor's consent.
Allowed whenever the officer has reasonable suspicion
Mere suspicion is not enough; Rule 113, Sec. 5 lists specific cases such as in flagrante, hot pursuit and escapees.
Allowed only for crimes punishable by over 6 years
Rule 113 does not depend on the penalty; it depends on the circumstances of the arrest.
Never allowed without prior court approval
Rule 113, Sec. 5 allows arrests without a warrant in specific cases.
Accusation in writing filed by the prosecutor
That is an information, not a complaint.
Unsworn report written by a police officer
A complaint must be sworn. A police report is not a complaint.
Order of the court directing an arrest
That is a warrant of arrest.
Sworn accusation by the offended party
That is a complaint, not an information.
Order issued by the court for arrest
That is a warrant of arrest.
Motion filed by the defense to dismiss
That is a motion to quash or to dismiss.
No person shall be compelled to testify against oneself
That is the right against self-incrimination.
No person shall be detained without charges
That is protection against arbitrary detention (Art. 125 RPC).
No person shall be punished by a law passed after the act
That is the ex post facto prohibition.
Procedural and Administrative
Administrative due process is a setting, not an aspect; the two aspects are substantive and procedural.
Substantive and Equitable
Equitable is not an aspect of due process; the second aspect is procedural.
Criminal and Civil
Those are kinds of cases, not aspects of due process.

keep: The correct answer is already the shortest option, and the wrong ones are real mitigating circumstances that students confuse with exempting ones.

wrong: The act is lawful, so there is neither crime nor liability
That describes justifying circumstances, where the act itself is lawful. With exempting circumstances there is a crime but no criminal liability.
Criminal liability but no civil liability
It is the reverse: the offender is exempt from criminal liability, but civil liability generally remains (Art. 101).
Penalty is lowered by one or two degrees
That is the effect of privileged mitigating circumstances.

keep: The correct answer is already the shortest option, and the wrong ones are the real justifying circumstances.
All options are about the same length, and the wrong ones are the other real elements of self-defense.

wrong: Defender is related to the person attacked
Relationship is required for defense of relatives, not of strangers.
Defender used the least harmful means available to stop the attack
Reasonable necessity of the means is shared by all three defenses; it is not the additional element for strangers.
Defender acted under orders of a superior
That is obedience to a superior order, a separate justifying circumstance.
Unlawful aggression, reasonable necessity, and the aggressor being a stranger
The relationship to the aggressor does not matter in self-defense; the third element is lack of sufficient provocation by the defender.
Unlawful aggression, proportionate weapon, lack of sufficient provocation
The law does not require equal weapons; it asks whether the means used was reasonably necessary.
Intent, motive, and opportunity to commit the act
Those are investigative concepts, not the elements of self-defense.
Crime is a free choice weighed against pleasure and pain
That is the classical school (Beccaria, Bentham).
Punishment should fit the crime, not the offender
That is classical thinking; positivists individualize treatment to the offender.
Crime is caused by possession by evil spirits
That is demonological thinking, which came before scientific criminology.

keep: Every option is a real penalty range in the same format; the correct one is not the longest.
Every option is a real penalty range in the same format, and the correct one is the shortest.
All four options are real RPC articles on crimes against persons and are the same length.

wrong: Presence of mitigating circumstances like voluntary surrender
Mitigating circumstances lower the penalty within a crime; they do not separate murder from homicide.
Relationship of the offender to the victim, like a spouse
Relationship makes the killing parricide.
Use of a deadly weapon such as a firearm
The kind of weapon used does not turn homicide into murder.
The person is named in a police blotter entry as a suspect in a crime committed several days earlier
Rule 113 requires personal knowledge of a crime that has just been committed; a blotter entry about an older crime is not enough.
The arresting officer received an anonymous tip that the person is carrying illegal drugs in a bag
An anonymous tip alone is not enough; the officer must personally see an overt act or have personal knowledge.
The person matches the general description of a suspect in a robbery that was committed in another city last month
A general description and an old crime elsewhere do not meet Rule 113, Sec. 5; a warrant is needed.
The body of the deceased victim
Corpus delicti means the body of the crime, the fact that a crime was committed, not the corpse.
Extrajudicial confession of the accused
A confession alone is not enough to convict without proof of the corpus delicti.
Proof of the identity of the person who committed the crime
The identity of the offender must also be proved, but it is separate from corpus delicti.
Admissible if relevant to the case
Relevance does not cure illegality; the Constitution (Art. III, Sec. 3) excludes such evidence.
Admissible but the officer is penalized
The Philippines applies the exclusionary rule, not just penalties for the officer.
Admissible once the case reaches trial
Illegally obtained evidence stays inadmissible at every stage.
Statements made believing death is imminent
That is a dying declaration.
Statements against one's own interest
That is a declaration against interest.
Opinions given by an expert witness
That is expert testimony, not res gestae.
Testimony of a witness who saw the crime
That is direct evidence, which needs no inference.
Evidence the court notices without proof
That is judicial notice.
Proof of the accused's past crimes
Evidence of past crimes is generally not admissible to prove the present one; it is not what circumstantial evidence means.
Out of court statements are always admissible if relevant
Relevance does not cure hearsay; such statements are generally excluded unless an exception applies.
Only statements written and signed are admissible
The rule is about out-of-court statements offered for their truth, written or not.
Statements made by the accused are never admissible
Admissions and confessions of the accused can be admitted; they are not barred by the hearsay rule.
Physical harm causing bodily injury
That is physical violence under RA 9262.
Forcing the woman to watch obscene material
That is sexual violence under RA 9262.
Depriving the woman of financial support legally due her
That is economic abuse under RA 9262.
